title: Immutability, Values and References
oneLiner: What assignment really copies: C# value types versus reference types, Python names for objects, mutable versus immutable, shallow versus deep copies, read-only views versus immutable collections, and == versus identity.
keyTakeaway: Assigning a C# struct copies the data; assigning a class, list or array copies only a reference, so both variables share one object. In Python every assignment shares the object, and what matters is whether the object can change. Copy before changing shared data, and remember a shallow copy still shares the inner objects.
explanation:
Many confusing bugs come down to one question: when I write b = a, do I get a copy, or a second name for the same thing? The basics track touched on this for function arguments; this lesson answers it fully.

C# splits types in two. A value type (int, double, bool, DateTime, any struct) holds its data directly, so assignment copies the data. A reference type (any class, string, arrays, List, Dictionary) lives on the heap and variables hold a reference to it, so assignment shares the object. Python is simpler: every variable is a name for an object, and assignment never copies. What differs is whether the object is mutable (lists, dicts, sets, most objects) or immutable (numbers, strings, tuples, frozenset).

Copying has two depths: a shallow copy makes a new outer container that still shares the inner objects, a deep copy duplicates everything. Immutability, objects that can't change after they're created, sidesteps the whole problem: there's nothing to protect if nobody can change anything. The lesson also separates truly immutable collections from read-only views, and "equal" (==) from "the same object" (ReferenceEquals, is).
